q: A perfect black body is a body that:
o: Reflects all the radiation that falls on it
Emits radiation of one wavelength only
Absorbs all the radiation that falls on it, whatever its wavelength
x: A black body absorbs every wavelength completely, reflecting none; it is also the best possible emitter at any temperature (a small hole in a hollow enclosure is a good model). It emits a continuous spectrum, not a single wavelength.

q: The temperature of a black body is raised. The wavelength at which it emits radiation with maximum intensity:
x: By Wien's displacement law λ_max T = constant, so a higher temperature gives a shorter λ_max. This is why a heated iron rod glows dull red first and then orange, yellow and white as it gets hotter.

q: The absolute temperature of a black body is doubled. The total energy it radiates per second from each square metre of its surface becomes:
x: By Stefan's law the power radiated per unit area is E = σT⁴, so doubling T multiplies it by 2⁴ = 16. Treating E as proportional to T² gives 4 times; to T³ gives 8 times.

q: To explain the black-body spectrum, Planck assumed that the oscillating atoms of the body can emit or absorb energy:
o: Only in whole-number multiples of hf
x: Planck's hypothesis was that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets (quanta), so the energy of an oscillator of frequency f can only be E = nhf with n = 1, 2, 3, … The classical idea of continuous energy exchange is what failed.

q: A black body at 2000 K radiates most strongly at 1.45 μm. It is heated until it radiates most strongly at 0.725 μm. The total power it radiates becomes:
x: Wien's law λ_max T = constant: halving λ_max means T doubles to 4000 K. By Stefan's law the power ∝ T⁴, so it rises by 2⁴ = 16. Stopping after Wien's law gives 2 times; using λ ∝ T gives ½.

q: Classical wave theory, which treats radiation energy as continuous, made a prediction about black-body radiation at short (ultraviolet) wavelengths that disagreed with experiment. It predicted that the intensity would:
o: Fall to zero at all wavelengths
Have a peak exactly where experiment shows one
Increase without limit as the wavelength gets shorter
Be the same at every wavelength
x: Classical theory predicted an intensity rising without limit towards short wavelengths (the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'), whereas experiment shows a peak and then a fall. Planck's quantum hypothesis removed this disagreement.

q: In a photoelectric experiment, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is plotted against the frequency of the light. The graph is a straight line whose slope is equal to:
o: The charge of the electron e
x: From K.E.max = hf − φ, the graph of K.E.max against f is a straight line of slope h. Its intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency f₀, and the intercept on the energy axis (extended) is −φ.

q: The fastest photoelectrons emitted from a metal have a kinetic energy of 2 eV. The stopping potential needed to stop all of them is:
x: The stopping potential V₀ satisfies eV₀ = K.E.max, so a K.E.max of 2 eV needs V₀ = 2 V. Writing 2 eV as 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and dropping the power of ten gives 3.2 V; halving or doubling the energy has no basis, since 1 eV is exactly the energy one electron gains through 1 V.

q: Light whose photons have an energy of 4 eV falls on a metal, and the stopping potential is 1.5 V. If the photon energy is raised to 5 eV, the stopping potential becomes:
x: Work function φ = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 eV. With 5 eV photons, K.E.max = 5 − 2.5 = 2.5 eV, so V₀ = 2.5 V. Scaling 1.5 V in the ratio 5/4 gives 1.875 V; using 5 − 1.5 gives 3.5 V.

q: A beam of light falls on a photocell connected in a circuit with a relay. A burglar alarm rings when a person walks through the beam because:
o: Blocking the light increases the photoelectric current
Blocking the light stops the photoelectric current in the photocell
The light changes its frequency when blocked
x: While light falls on the cathode, photoelectrons give a current that holds the relay; when the beam is cut, emission and the current stop, and the relay switches on the alarm. The person does not change the light's frequency.

q: Photoelectrons are emitted almost instantly (within about 10⁻⁹ s) even when very dim light of suitable frequency falls on a metal. This observation supports the idea that:
o: Light energy arrives in packets (photons), each absorbed by a single electron
Light energy is spread evenly over the wave front
Electrons need time to collect energy from the light wave
The work function falls when light is dim
x: In wave theory dim light would need time for an electron to collect enough energy; in the photon picture a single photon gives all its energy hf to one electron at once, so emission is immediate. The work function is a property of the metal, not of the light.

q: Photons of energy 3 eV fall on a metal of work function 2 eV. The maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons is about: (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
x: K.E.max = 3 − 2 = 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 9.1 × 10⁻³¹) = √(3.5 × 10¹¹) ≈ 5.9 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the 2 gives 4.2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; using the work function 2 eV as the kinetic energy gives 8.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, and using the photon energy 3 eV gives 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

q: The Compton effect, in which X-ray photons lose energy when scattered by electrons, is strong evidence that photons:
o: Carry momentum and collide like particles
x: Compton explained the wavelength shift by treating the photon as a particle with momentum h/λ colliding elastically with an electron, conserving energy and momentum. Photons have zero rest mass and travel at c.

q: For an electron, h/m₀c = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m. The largest possible increase in wavelength of an X-ray photon Compton-scattered by a free electron is:
x: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) is greatest at θ = 180°, where 1 − cos θ = 2, so Δλmax = 2 × 2.4 × 10⁻¹² = 4.8 × 10⁻¹² m. Taking θ = 90° gives 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m; zero shift happens at θ = 0°.

q: A high-energy gamma-ray photon can change into an electron-positron pair only when it passes close to a heavy nucleus, not in empty space. The nucleus is needed mainly to:
o: Supply the charge of the electron
Supply the rest-mass energy of the pair
Take up some momentum so that momentum is conserved
Slow the photon down below the speed of light
x: In empty space a photon cannot turn into a pair while conserving both energy and momentum; a nearby nucleus recoils and takes the extra momentum, while taking very little energy. The pair's charges cancel (−e and +e), and the energy comes from the photon itself.

q: The Compton shift is easy to observe with X-rays but practically impossible to see with visible light. The reason is that:
o: Visible light photons are not scattered by electrons at all
The shift is much smaller for long wavelengths
The shift, at most a few picometres, is a tiny fraction of a visible wavelength of about 500 nm
x: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) is at most about 5 × 10⁻¹² m whatever the wavelength. For X-rays of about 10⁻¹¹ m this is a large fraction, but for 5 × 10⁻⁷ m light it is only about 1 part in 10⁵. The shift does not depend on the wavelength, and visible photons do have momentum h/λ.

q: An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. They must have the same:
x: λ = h/p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. Since the proton is about 1836 times heavier, its speed must be correspondingly smaller, and its kinetic energy p²/2m is also smaller.

q: An electron starting from rest is accelerated through a potential difference of 150 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is about: (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: p = √(2meV) = √(2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 150) = √(4.37 × 10⁻⁴⁷) ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹, so λ = h/p ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the spacing of atoms in a crystal. Leaving out the 2 in √(2meV) gives 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

q: A cricket ball in flight does not show any noticeable wave behaviour such as diffraction because:
o: It has no de Broglie wavelength at all
Its de Broglie wavelength is far too long
Its large momentum makes its de Broglie wavelength extremely small
Only charged particles have wave properties
x: λ = h/(mv), and with a mass of about 0.16 kg and speeds of tens of m s⁻¹, λ is of order 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small for any gap or obstacle to diffract it. Every moving body has a de Broglie wavelength, charged or not.

q: The accelerating voltage of an electron microscope is increased. Its ability to show fine detail (resolving power) improves because the electrons':
x: A higher voltage gives the electrons more momentum, and λ = h/p becomes shorter; a shorter wavelength means less diffraction blurring and finer resolved detail. The electron's charge is fixed, and its mass does not fall.

q: Besides position and momentum, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle also applies to the pair of quantities:
o: Wavelength and frequency of light in a vacuum
x: The second form of the principle is ΔE Δt ≈ h: the energy of a state cannot be known exactly in a very short time. Wavelength and frequency of light are linked exactly by c = fλ, so they are not an uncertainty pair.

q: The position of a 0.1 kg ball is known to within 1 mm. Using Δx Δp ≈ h with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the uncertainty in its speed is about:
x: Δv = h/(mΔx) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.1 × 1 × 10⁻³) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁰ m s⁻¹, far too small to notice, which is why the principle matters only for tiny particles. 6.63 × 10⁻³¹ is Δp (not divided by the mass); taking Δx as 1 m gives 6.63 × 10⁻³³.

q: Two excited states of an atom have lifetimes of 10⁻⁸ s and 10⁻³ s. Compared with the spectral line from the long-lived state, the line from the short-lived state is:
o: Broader, because the energy of a short-lived state is less certain
Narrower, because the energy of a short-lived state is more certain
x: From ΔE Δt ≈ h, a shorter lifetime Δt means a larger energy spread ΔE, so the emitted photons have a wider range of frequencies and the line is broader. The long-lived (metastable) state gives a very sharp line.

q: An electron and a proton are each confined to the same region of width Δx. The proton's mass is 1836 times the electron's. Using Δx Δp ≈ h, the ratio (uncertainty in the electron's speed)/(uncertainty in the proton's speed) is about:
x: Both have the same Δp ≈ h/Δx, and Δv = Δp/m, so Δv is inversely proportional to the mass: Δv_e/Δv_p = m_p/m_e = 1836. Inverting the ratio gives 1/1836; equal Δp does not mean equal Δv.
